web_title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples
book_title: Chapter 2: Inside the Factory — Energy Turbines, Aerospace Propulsion & Concrete Part Economics
question: What exact products does Azad Engineering manufacture across its Energy, Oil & Gas, and Aerospace & Defence segments, how does the revenue mix break down, and how does a single part move from raw superalloy to a qualified turbine?

epigraph.quote: A turbine blade is not a piece of metal; it is an aerodynamic sculpture machined to micron tolerances out of an alloy specifically designed to resist being cut.
epigraph.author: Precision Machining Principle

web_blocks.title: Revenue & Order-Book Mix: Export-Led Power & Propulsion

web_blocks.html: Azad Engineering is a pure-play Tier-1 maker of mission-critical and life-critical precision parts. It reports across two core verticals: Energy & Oil & Gas, and Aerospace & Defence [2][4][5]. Exports drive roughly ~93% of revenue across Japan, Europe, and North America. Domestic Indian sales contribute about ~7%, though defence propulsion and BHEL orders are growing [3][4]. FY26 consolidated revenue hit ₹603 Cr, and TTM Sep 2026 sales reached ₹684 Cr. Behind those sales sits a rolling order book of roughly ₹6,500 Cr (~10–11x annual sales), backed by over ₹3,200 Cr in disclosed long-term OEM contracts [1][3][10].

web_blocks.takeaway: Energy & Oil & Gas remains the volume and cash-generation backbone (~80% of sales), while Aerospace & Defence (~17–20%) provides high-margin diversification and strategic optionality in complete small-thrust jet engines.

web_blocks.title: Segment 1: Energy & Oil & Gas (~79–80% of Revenue) — Concrete End-to-End Example

web_blocks.html: The Energy & Oil & Gas unit supplies rotating and stationary airfoils, buckets, nozzle vanes, and combustion parts. These serve heavy-duty gas turbines, steam turbines, nuclear power islands, and oilfield drilling systems [4][11][12]. Consider Azad's single-source 8-year Long-Term Contract and Price Agreement (LTCPA) with Mitsubishi Heavy Industries (MHI), Japan. It covers hot-section nozzle vane segments and advanced gas/thermal turbine airfoils. That deal sits within a cumulative MHI relationship topping $156 million / ~₹1,387 Cr [12].

The Customer Problem: MHI's high-efficiency gas turbines run at firing temperatures above 1,600°C. That heat maximizes combined-cycle plant output for global grid and data-center power demand. At those temperatures, hot-section nozzle vanes guide supersonic, corrosive combustion gases onto rotating blades. Even a 10-micron profile error or micro-crack cuts aerodynamic efficiency or causes blade-tip rub. MHI needed a dedicated non-Japanese Tier-1 partner that could hold tight tolerances without single-region bottlenecks [12].

From Raw Alloy to Qualified Part: Azad buys certified nickel-based superalloy forgings or bar stock, such as Inconel 718 / Waspaloy. Those alloys resist heat and deformation, so they work-harden and wear down standard cutting tools. Inside its dedicated 7,200 sq. m. MHI facility at Tuniki Bollaram (commissioned March 2025) [16], blanks enter simultaneous 5-axis CNC milling. Single-setup milling carves 3D twisted airfoil contours without fixture stack-up errors, holding tolerances to ±0.005 mm (5 microns). Parts then pass through NADCAP-compliant stress-relief heat treatment and precision surface finishing. Next come coordinate measuring machine (CMM) laser scans and ultrasonic/fluorescent penetrant non-destructive testing (NDT). Multi-year rate contracts lock in pricing with raw-material pass-through clauses, yielding mid-30s segment EBITDA margins [12][15]. A similar model serves Siemens Energy (€90.1 million / ~₹811 Cr, 6-year deal for combustion commodities, cold blades, and vanes) [11]. It also covers GE Vernova (three exclusive 7,600 sq. m. plants for steam/nuclear/industrial airfoils) [16][17] and Baker Hughes (7,600 sq. m. plant commissioned April 2026 for complex oilfield parts) [16].

web_blocks.title: Segment 2: Aerospace & Defence (~17–20% of Revenue) — Concrete End-to-End Example

web_blocks.html: Azad's Aerospace & Defence unit makes precision-forged and 5-axis machined rotating engine parts and flight-critical airframe hardware. These parts fly on Boeing 737/777, Airbus A320/A350, and Gulfstream jets for Rolls-Royce, Honeywell, and Eaton. Azad also serves domestic defence programs with HAL and DRDO [10][13]. For years, Azad acted strictly as a build-to-print component supplier. In 2025–2026, it made a structural leap with India's Gas Turbine Research Establishment (GTRE) under DRDO [13].

Concrete End-to-End Example — The Indigenous ATGG Expendable Turbojet Engine: India's cruise missiles, loitering munitions, and target drones once relied on imported small-thrust turbojet engines. That reliance created strategic and export-control risks. GTRE designed an indigenous Advanced Turbo Gas Generator (ATGG) expendable turbojet engine in the 350 kgf (3.4 kN) thrust class. It picked Azad Engineering as its private-sector manufacturing and integration partner [13]. Unlike a single turbine blade order, this program required Azad to machine high-speed compressor and turbine rotors from titanium (Ti-6Al-4V) and superalloys. Azad also balanced the spool assembly to sub-micron runout limits, integrated fuel-control and ignition subsystems, and delivered a flight-ready propulsion unit [13].

Azad built, assembled, and delivered the first indigenous ATGG turbojet engine to GTRE/DRDO [13]. Early defence engine deliveries add modest initial revenue next to the ₹603 Cr consolidated base. Yet the strategic shift is clear: Azad proved it can move from a parts vendor to a complete propulsion system integrator. Once weapon-testing and airworthiness checks conclude, serial builds for domestic tactical missiles and UAVs can diversify Azad's 93% export mix [13].

web_blocks.title: Segment Economics: Why 37% Operating Margins Exist
web_blocks.text: Notice the financial signature of these two segments: Cost of materials consumed in FY26 was just ₹57.04 Cr on ₹590.38 Cr standalone revenue (~9.7% of sales) [14]. Why is raw material cost so low relative to revenue? Because in many OEM turbine contracts, Azad either receives customer-supplied forgings or adds immense machining, engineering, and certification value onto exotic alloys—with employee costs (₹131.02 Cr) and specialized tooling/power/overhead (₹184.56 Cr) representing the true conversion engine [14].

web_blocks.title: Why Rotating Parts Differ from Static Castings or Airframes

web_blocks.html: Investors comparing Indian precision firms should note the physical stress profile of Azad's parts. Static airframe brackets or hydraulic manifolds face predictable structural loads. By contrast, 3D rotating airfoils and turbine buckets spin at thousands of RPM inside hot, corrosive gas or steam flows [2][5]. Azad's value-add lies in multi-axis toolpath engineering, residual-stress control, and zero-defect metrology across 1,700+ qualified SKUs [5]. Two new 7,600 sq. m. exclusive GE Vernova plants opened in September 2026 [17], alongside the April 2026 Baker Hughes oilfield plant [16]. Together, these launches show OEMs are expanding wallet share across steam, gas, nuclear, and downhole Oil & Gas hardware. That multi-plant commitment reduces single-customer ramp risk over time. Each dedicated bay locks in multi-year tooling, metrology, and engineering routines.

book_paragraphs: To really grasp what happens inside Azad Engineering's shop floors in Hyderabad, you and I need to strip away the buzzwords and follow two actual pieces of metal from raw bar stock to final inspection. Because at the end of the day, Azad is not a software platform or a brand; it is a precision conversion machine that turns hard-to-cut superalloys into rotating hardware under two main roofs: Energy and Oil & Gas, which drives roughly 79 to 80 percent of revenue, and Aerospace and Defence, which accounts for the remaining 17 to 20 percent.

Start with the Energy division, which exports over ninety percent of its output to global power giants like Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, and Baker Hughes. Think about what Mitsubishi Heavy Industries faces when it builds a modern combined-cycle gas turbine. To squeeze maximum electricity out of every unit of fuel—especially as data centers and industrial grids demand reliable baseload power—combustion gases inside the turbine hot section exceed 1,600 degrees Celsius. Sitting directly in that supersonic blast of heat are stationary nozzle vanes and rotating turbine blades.

Those vanes cannot be stamped or cast casually. If a single contour is off by ten microns—a fraction of the width of a human hair—aerodynamic efficiency drops, or worse, a blade expands under heat and shears off the casing. Under an eight-year, single-source contract with MHI, Azad takes certified nickel-based superalloys like Inconel 718 and Waspaloy—metals specifically invented to resist melting or bending, which means they fight back fiercely against cutting tools. Inside a dedicated 7,200-square-meter MHI plant at Tuniki Bollaram, five-axis CNC machines carve the twisted three-dimensional airfoil geometry in a single continuous setup, holding tolerances around five microns. Every vane then goes through NADCAP-accredited heat treatment, coordinate-measuring laser scans, and ultrasonic flaw detection before it ever earns an export stamp.

Now walk across to the Aerospace and Defence division, where Azad makes rotating engine hardware for Rolls-Royce, Honeywell, Eaton, and commercial platforms like the Boeing 737 and Airbus A320. For fifteen years, Azad was strictly a build-to-print component supplier: the OEM handed over a blueprint, and Azad delivered a qualified part. But recently, Azad crossed a threshold that very few Indian private manufacturers have reached. Partnering with DRDO's Gas Turbine Research Establishment, Azad manufactured, assembled, and delivered India's first indigenous expendable turbojet engine—the 350-kilogram-force ATGG unit designed for cruise missiles and target drones.

Think about the difference between machining a single titanium blade and delivering a complete jet engine. In the ATGG program, Azad had to machine the compressor and turbine rotors, dynamically balance the spinning spool to sub-micron tolerances, integrate the fuel and ignition subsystems, and hand over a working propulsion unit. Early deliveries do not move the ₹603 crore revenue needle overnight, but they prove Azad can move up the value chain from parts vendor to propulsion system integrator—while also building a domestic defence pillar to balance its 93 percent export skew.

It is also worth noting how the Energy and Oil & Gas division itself is diversifying internally. Beyond Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, Azad commissioned a dedicated 7,200-square-meter plant for Siemens Energy under a six-year, €90.1 million contract covering combustion commodities, cold blades, and vanes. It operates three exclusive 7,600-square-meter facilities for GE Vernova—two of them inaugurated as recently as September 28, 2026—serving steam, industrial, and nuclear power turbines. And in April 2026, it launched a 7,600-square-meter lean manufacturing plant for Baker Hughes to scale complex oilfield and downhole components.

When you step back and look at both segments together, you see why Azad's gross value addition is so high. Whether a part is spinning inside a Siemens gas turbine in Europe, a GE Vernova steam island in North America, a Baker Hughes downhole tool, or an indigenous DRDO cruise-missile engine, the common denominator is the same: exotic alloys, micron-level five-axis machining, and multi-year qualification lock-in.

Notice what this segment mix means for the durability—and cyclicality—of Azad's revenue base. Roughly three-quarters to four-fifths of sales still come from Energy and Oil & Gas rotating equipment, where global gas-turbine and steam-turbine builds are enjoying a powerful multi-year cycle driven by grid reliability and AI data-center power demand. Aerospace and Defence currently contributes roughly 15% to 20% of revenue, yet it carries the longest qualification runway and highest strategic optionality—anchored by Rolls-Royce, Honeywell, Eaton, HAL, and the GTRE 350 kgf turbojet engine program. Because over 93% of revenue is exported across Europe, North America, and Japan, Azad effectively operates as a global Tier-1 precision supplier domiciled in Hyderabad, enjoying global engineering economics while bearing export-corridor working-capital cycles.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: Why Material Costs Are Under 10% of Revenue
book_callouts.text: If you glance at Azad's FY26 standalone P&L, one number will jump off the page: Cost of Materials Consumed was only ₹57 crore against ₹590 crore of revenue—less than 10 percent. That tells you everything about the business model. You are not buying a metal trader; you are looking at pure engineering value-addition, where skilled machinists, five-axis toolpaths, and zero-defect certification capture the vast majority of the sales rupee.

book_callouts.title: MENTAL MODEL: Single-Source LTCPA Stickiness
book_callouts.text: Once an OEM like MHI or Siemens Energy qualifies a supplier for a hot-section airfoil and dedicates an entire 7,200 sq. m. bay to that program, switching vendors mid-contract is practically impossible. Re-qualifying a replacement supplier takes 3 to 5 years and millions of dollars in rig testing—giving the incumbent deep multi-year revenue visibility.

book_subsections.title: Inside a Hot-Section Blade Order: From Billet to Final CMM Sign-Off
paragraphs: To make Azad's business model tangible, walk with me through a single steam- or gas-turbine airfoil order from start to finish. It begins not with a purchase order, but with a three-to-five-year First Article Inspection cycle. The OEM—say Siemens Energy or Mitsubishi Heavy Industries—supplies a certified superalloy specification (often Inconel 718, titanium Ti-6Al-4V, or martensitic stainless steel) and an engineering drawing with tolerances measured in single-digit microns. Every curve of the twisted three-dimensional airfoil determines aerodynamic efficiency inside a turbine spinning at 3,000 to 10,000 revolutions per minute under extreme thermal stress.

Once qualified, Azad's Hyderabad team forges or machines the blank on multi-axis CNC milling centers, performs specialized heat treatment and non-destructive testing—ultrasonic, fluorescent penetrant, and X-ray inspection under NADCAP-accredited protocols—and verifies every geometric coordinate on automated Coordinate Measuring Machines. Only after complete metallurgical traceability is logged from raw bar stock to finished serial number does the batch ship to Europe, Japan, or North America. That painstaking verification chain explains both why Azad's operating margins reach 37% to 38% and why work-in-progress inventory sits on the floor for months at a time.
